meta.blurb: A shy Mole leaves his spring cleaning and finds the river, a loyal Rat and a vain, car-mad Toad. Through snowy woods, a night of strange music and a battle for Toad Hall, four friends learn what home and friendship are worth.
meta.bible: Mole: a shy, gentle animal who leaves his spring cleaning and finds the river. Rat (Water Rat): Mole's friend, who loves the river and boats and writes poems. Toad: the rich, vain, boastful owner of Toad Hall, who takes up one craze after another. Badger (Mr Badger): a wise, gruff, kind old animal who lives in the Wild Wood. Otter: Rat's friend; Portly is his young son. Pan: the great gentle god of the wild, seen on the island. Sea Rat: a sailor rat from the southern harbours. Chief Weasel: the leader of the Wild Wooders. Toad Hall: Toad's grand house by the river. The Wild Wood: the dark wood beyond the fields. Mole End: Mole's old home. The river bank. England. Fixed facts: Mole bumps into Rat on the first day of spring; Toad's caravan is wrecked by a motor car; Toad steals a car and is sentenced to twenty years in prison; he escapes dressed as a washerwoman; the Wild Wooders (weasels, stoats and ferrets) take Toad Hall; a secret tunnel leads from the river bank into the Hall. Voice and tone: warm, gentle and humorous, with a love of the countryside and the seasons; adventure without gore; friendship and home are the heart of the book; the animals talk and wear clothes, as in the original by Kenneth Grahame.

A1A2: Mole was tired of cleaning his house, so he ran outside.
In the warm sun, Mole walked across a field and found a river.
By the river Mole met Rat, and Rat took him out in a boat.
Rat loved the river and said, “There is nothing better than boats.”
They had lunch in the boat, with chicken, bread and cold drinks.
Mole wanted to row, but he made the boat turn over.
Rat laughed, and then he took Mole to his warm home.
Rat took Mole to see Toad, who lived in a big house.
Toad showed them his new yellow wagon and wanted them to come.
The three friends travelled slowly along the road, and Toad was very happy.
A fast car scared the horse, and the wagon fell over.
Toad sat on the road and dreamed only of cars.
In winter, Mole wanted to meet Badger, but Rat said Badger was very shy.
One cold day Mole went alone into the dark Wild Wood.
Mole heard strange sounds and saw faces, so he hid in an old tree.
Rat found Mole, and the two friends began to walk home through the snow.
In the snow, Mole fell over something, and they found a hidden door.
Badger opened the door, and at first he looked cross, but soon he smiled.
Badger gave them hot food and told them about his home under the ground.
Next morning Badger took them home by a secret path, and spoke about Toad.
On a winter walk Mole smelled his old home and began to cry.
Rat came back, and together they found Mole's little home under the ground.
Some small field mice sang songs at the door, and Mole gave them food.
Mole ate supper with his friends and slept happily in his own bed.
Toad crashed many cars, so Badger, Rat and Mole decided to stop him.
They went to Toad Hall and locked him in his bedroom.
Toad pretended to be ill, and then he climbed out of the window.
Toad stole a car and drove fast, and the police caught him.
The judge sent Toad to a dark prison for twenty years.
A kind girl at the prison felt sorry for Toad and helped him.
Toad put on an old woman's dress and walked out of the prison.
Toad rode a train, but the police chased it, so he jumped off.
In summer, Otter's little son was lost, and Rat and Mole went to look.
All night they rowed on the river and heard sweet music at dawn.
On an island they found the little otter asleep beside a kind god.
A boat woman learned who Toad was, so he ran away on her horse.
Toad sold the horse to a man for money and bought a big breakfast.
Toad got into a car, drove too fast, and crashed into a pond.
In autumn, the birds flew south, and Rat felt a strong wish to go.
A sailor rat visited Rat and told him wonderful stories about the sea.
Rat wanted to go with the sailor, but Mole stopped him kindly.
Toad found Rat, and Rat said bad animals now lived in Toad Hall.
Toad cried, but Badger said they must be clever and brave.
Mole went out in a disguise and learned about a party at Toad Hall.
Badger knew a secret way under the ground into Toad Hall.
That night the four friends walked through the dark tunnel under Toad Hall.
Above them the weasels had a loud party, and the friends waited quietly.
Suddenly the friends ran up the stairs, and the weasels were very afraid.
The weasels ran away, and Toad Hall was Toad's home again.
Toad gave a big party, and he promised to be a better friend.
B1B2: Mole had spent the whole morning cleaning his small home under the ground, and he was thoroughly tired of it. Suddenly he threw down his brush and ran up through the earth into the warm spring sunshine.
The meadow was full of birds, and Mole felt as though he had been shut up for years. Soon he came to a wide, shining river, which he had never seen before in his life.
On the bank he met Rat, a friendly water animal, who invited him into a little blue boat. They pushed off, and Mole sat in a boat for the very first time.
Rat told him that the river was his whole world, and that he needed nothing else. “There is nothing half so good as simply messing about in boats,” he said.
Rat had brought a large basket, and soon the two friends were eating cold chicken, bread and salad on the water. Mole had never been so happy, and he listened to every word the river seemed to say.
Mole begged to row, and although Rat warned him, he grabbed the oars and tried. A moment later the boat turned over, and both of them fell into the cold water.
Rat laughed kindly, pulled Mole to the bank, and dried him by a warm fire in his riverside home. Mole was so comfortable there that he decided to stay, and the two animals became firm friends.
One sunny day Rat took Mole to meet Toad, who lived in a grand house called Toad Hall. Toad was very rich and good-natured, but he was also vain and could never stay interested in one thing for long.
Toad's newest craze was a bright yellow caravan, pulled by a cream-coloured horse, and he begged his friends to join him. Rat did not want to go, but Toad's excitement was so great that he gave in.

The three of them set off along the dusty road, and Toad talked proudly about the adventures that lay ahead. Mole enjoyed every moment, and in the evening they stopped for the night beside a quiet field.
Suddenly a motor car roared past them, and the frightened horse ran wild. The caravan crashed over and lay in a ditch with its wheels in the air.
Toad sat in the dust with a faraway look, whispering the sound of the car's horn again and again. From that day on he dreamed of nothing but motor cars, and Rat was very cross.
When winter came, Mole often thought of Badger, who lived in the great Wild Wood beyond the fields. Rat said that Badger hated visitors and never came to see anyone, so Mole would have to wait.
One cold afternoon, while Rat was dozing by the fire, Mole crept out alone and walked into the Wild Wood. At first it was only a place of snow and bare trees, and he felt quite brave.
Then the light faded, and he saw small, wicked faces peering at him from holes among the roots. A strange whistling rose behind him, and in terror he hid inside an old tree.

Meanwhile Rat woke, found Mole gone, and followed his small footprints into the wood with a stout stick and a pair of pistols. When he found his friend shaking in the old tree, he spoke gently and promised to take him home.
Snow began to fall thickly, and the two friends lost their way among the trees. Then Mole hurt his leg on an iron boot-scraper, and beside it they found a small door under the snow.
Rat rang the bell, and after a long wait a gruff voice asked who was there so late. Badger opened the door, looked cross, and then welcomed them warmly when he saw who they were.
In his big warm kitchen Badger gave them dry clothes and a hot supper. He told them that the Wild Wood had once been a busy city, and that his tunnels lay beneath it.
In the morning Badger led his guests through a long tunnel and out near the edge of the wood. Before they parted he promised that he would deal with Toad when spring came.
Weeks later, as the two friends walked home along a frosty lane, Mole suddenly smelled the scent of his old home. He stopped and began to sob, and Rat, who was walking ahead, turned back in alarm.
Rat listened kindly, and together they hurried back until they found the little door of Mole's old home under the ground. Inside it was dusty and cold, but Mole was glad to see his own things again.
Soon a group of small field mice stood outside in the snow and sang a Christmas song. Mole and Rat asked them in for a warm drink and sent them away happy with food.
Then Mole and Rat sat down to a simple supper, and Mole felt proud of his little house. That night he slept in his own bed, glad that he had both his friends and his home.

Months later Toad had bought one motor car after another and crashed every one of them. One morning Badger arrived at the river and told Rat and Mole that they must stop Toad before somebody was hurt.

The three friends went to Toad Hall, where they found Toad dressed in a grand new coat for driving. Badger spoke to him sternly, but Toad would not promise to give up cars, so they locked him in his bedroom.
Rat and the others guarded him in turn, but Toad pretended to be very ill and begged for a doctor. As soon as Rat went to fetch one, Toad tied his sheets together and climbed out of the window.
Free again, Toad strolled into a village inn, where he saw a splendid motor car standing in the yard. He could not resist it, so he stole the car and raced away at terrible speed.
The police soon caught him, and the judge found him guilty of stealing the car and driving dangerously. He had also been very rude to the police, so he was sent to a dark prison for twenty years.
Alone in his dungeon, Toad wept and felt sure that he would never see his friends again. But the jailer's daughter felt sorry for him and brought him tea and kind words.
The girl had an aunt who washed clothes, and she lent Toad the old woman's dress and shawl. Dressed like a washerwoman, Toad walked boldly past the guards, and nobody stopped him.
Toad had too little money for a ticket, but a kind engine driver let him ride on the engine. Police chased the train, so Toad jumped off in the dark and hid in the fields.
In high summer, Otter's little son Portly did not come home, and his father was very worried. Rat and Mole promised to search the river for him, and they set out in the evening.
They rowed all night under the stars, calling softly and listening to the water. Just before dawn, Rat heard a sweet, wild music that seemed to pull them towards a small island.

On the island they saw the great god Pan and found the little otter asleep at his feet. Afterwards they forgot what they had seen, for the god gave them forgetfulness so that they would not be troubled.
Meanwhile Toad, still in his dress, accepted a lift on a canal boat pulled by a horse. The woman asked him to wash some clothes, but he was so clumsy that she soon guessed the truth.
After a fierce quarrel, Toad rode off on the horse that pulled the boat, laughing at his own cleverness. Later he sold the horse to a traveller and spent the money on a big breakfast.
Soon a motor car stopped beside him, and its owners offered the tired old washerwoman a ride. Toad could not resist taking the wheel, and he drove so wildly that the car plunged into a pond.
Autumn came, and the swallows gathered in noisy crowds, ready to fly away to the south. Rat watched them with a strange longing, for the warm lands seemed to be calling to him.
One evening a Sea Rat arrived, tired and dusty from the road, and told wonderful tales of ships and harbours. Rat listened with shining eyes, and his heart filled with dreams of distant ports.
Next morning Rat packed a bag and prepared to follow the Sea Rat to the south. Mole held him firmly until the spell was broken, and soon Rat was happily writing a poem.
One cold evening a tired, muddy Toad knocked at Rat's door, and Rat took him in at once. Over a hot meal Toad heard with horror that weasels and stoats from the Wild Wood had taken over Toad Hall.
Toad burst into tears, for his beautiful home was full of enemies and he had nowhere to go. Badger came to join them and said that, although they were few, they could win with careful planning.
Mole put on a disguise and crept out to spy on Toad Hall and listen to the weasels. He came back with the news that the guards were careless and that the weasels were planning a big party.
Badger explained that a secret tunnel ran from the river bank all the way into Toad Hall. Toad was amazed, because in all his years there he had never heard of it.
That night the four friends took their sticks and crept into the tunnel, which was damp, dark and very long. Toad wanted to lead the way, but Badger told him firmly to keep close and quiet.

At the end they climbed some steps and heard the noise of the feast right above their heads. The weasels and stoats were singing and banging the tables, and nobody knew that four enemies waited below.
At Badger's signal the four friends burst into the hall with a great shout, waving their sticks. The startled weasels and stoats screamed and fell over one another as they tried to escape.
Soon the Wild Wooders had fled through the doors and windows, and Toad Hall belonged to its owner again. The friends were tired but happy, and Toad looked proudly round at his own beautiful hall.
The next day they held a splendid banquet, and the four friends laughed and talked far into the night. Toad had learned his lesson at last, and from then on he was a quieter, kinder and wiser animal.
C1C2: Mole had spent the whole morning scrubbing and sweeping his small, dark home beneath the ground until he could bear it no longer. Spring was stirring somewhere overhead, and its restless message seemed to travel down through the very earth he stood upon. With a sudden cry of impatience he flung away his brush, abandoned the whitewash and scrambled up the long tunnel into the open air.

The meadow lay warm and bright before him, loud with birds and soft with new grass, and Mole felt like a prisoner who had at last been let out of jail. He wandered on from hedge to hedge, drunk with sunshine, and laughed aloud at his own foolishness in having stayed indoors for so long. At length he came upon a broad, glittering river, a creature of moving light that he had never seen in all his days.

Seated on the bank, Mole noticed a hole in the opposite shore, and presently a pair of bright eyes peered out, then a whiskered face, and at last the whole sleek figure of Rat. Rat greeted the stranger with perfect good humour and, before Mole quite understood what was happening, had coaxed him down into a small blue boat. Mole had never set foot in a boat before, yet he took his seat with the shy delight of one who is about to be introduced to a new world.

As they glided downstream, Rat declared that the river was everything to him: it was his farm, his garden, his market and his neighbourhood, and he asked for nothing beyond it. Mole listened in amazement, trailing a paw in the cool water and drinking in the sounds of reeds, ripples and distant birds. “Believe me, there is nothing in the world half so pleasant as messing about in boats,” said Rat with a dreamy smile.

Presently Rat steered towards a shady bank and produced a great wicker hamper, packed with cold chicken, ham, salad, fresh rolls and enough ginger beer to last the whole afternoon. Mole, who had not known that a lunch could be so splendid, ate with the eager silence of the truly contented. All around them the water chuckled against the hull, as though the river itself were sharing in their small celebration.

Overcome by high spirits, Mole decided that he too must try the oars, and he leapt up in spite of Rat's anxious warning. The boat rocked, swung sideways and, with a single wild plunge, tipped both of them headlong into the river. Mole came up gasping and thoroughly ashamed, while Rat, who swam as easily as he walked, caught hold of him and towed him ashore, laughing so much that he could hardly speak.

Dripping and miserable, Mole was led to Rat's snug riverside home, where a bright fire, dry clothes and a hearty supper soon restored his spirits. Rat assured him, with real kindness, that the best of friends are those who forgive such accidents, and that there was room in the house for as long as he chose to stay. By the end of that first day, Mole had found not only a river but the companion whose company would colour all the seasons to come.

Some weeks later, on a golden morning, Rat rowed his friend upstream to call on Toad, whose great house of mellow red brick stood in its own beautiful grounds above the water. Toad was enormously rich and kind-hearted, though he was also so vain and boastful that his friends had long since learned to smile at him. His only real fault, as Rat put it, was that he took up one craze after another with passionate enthusiasm and dropped each of them just as quickly.

His latest passion was a travelling caravan, a gaily painted yellow wagon with red wheels, a little stove, a cupboard and a cheerful cream-coloured horse to draw it. Toad insisted that Rat and Mole must come with him along the open road that very afternoon, and he spoke so fervently of the joys of travel that Mole's eyes shone. Rat, who knew from experience how soon Toad's passions faded, held back for some time, but in the end he gave way to the pleading of the other two.

So the little party set out through the gates, the dust rising softly behind the wheels and the hedgerows heavy with the scents of summer. Toad chattered happily of the wonders that lay ahead, while Mole walked at the horse's head, feeling that life had never offered him anything half so delightful. When evening came they supped in the open under the stars and then climbed into their narrow beds, tired, contented and quite unaware of the disaster that lay ahead.

Before long a faint, far-off warning drifted along the road, and before anyone could think, a gleaming motor car came hurtling out of a cloud of dust, its horn blaring and its wheels hardly touching the ground. The horse reared in terror, plunged across the verge and dragged the caravan into the ditch, where it lay wrecked on its side, its bright yellow paint scratched and splintered. Rat shook his fist and shouted after the vanishing car, but the thunder of its engine had already faded into silence.

In the middle of the road sat Toad, his legs stretched out and his eyes fixed on the distant dust cloud, murmuring in tones of the deepest reverence the sound that the horn had made. To him the wrecked caravan was already forgotten, and the whole world, he declared, had narrowed to a single splendid thing, the motor car. Rat, who had hoped to bring his friend to his senses, stared at him in dismay, for he feared that this new craze might prove far more dangerous than any that had gone before.

Winter settled over the countryside, and the river grew black and sullen between banks of frost, while Rat spent much of every day dozing by the fire. Mole, whose thoughts kept straying towards the grey blur of the Wild Wood on the horizon, longed to meet its most famous inhabitant, old Mr Badger. Rat, however, warned that Badger disliked company and was not to be called upon by anyone, so Mole must wait, he said, until Badger chose to appear.

One bitter afternoon, while Rat slumbered in his armchair, Mole could resist no longer; he buttoned his coat, slipped out of the door and tramped across the white fields towards the dark line of the trees. At first the wood was merely sombre and silent, its bare branches laced with snow, and Mole advanced with something very like confidence. Yet the daylight was failing, the shadows were deepening, and with every step the place seemed to close behind him like a trap.

Then the faces began: small, sharp, wicked little faces that glared from the holes between the roots and vanished the moment he turned to look. A thin whistling rose from somewhere behind him, and then a soft, quick patter, as of many feet, that seemed to run beside him in the dark. Panic seized Mole at last, and he plunged blindly among the trees until he found a hollow in an ancient trunk, where he crept in, shaking, to wait for whatever might come.

Rat, meanwhile, had woken to find the fireside empty, and he guessed the truth at once. He thrust a pair of pistols into his belt, seized a stout stick and hurried across the snow, following the small tracks that led him straight into the wood. When at last he found his friend, huddled and trembling inside the tree, he uttered no word of blame; he only said, with great kindness, that it was time to go home.

The snow, however, now began to fall in thick, blinding flakes, and every path and landmark was blotted out until the two friends could not tell whether they were going forward or in circles. Presently Mole tripped over something hard and cut his shin sharply, and Rat, bending to examine it, grew excited, for it was an iron scraper of the kind placed beside a door. Together they scraped away the snow, and there, in the bank beneath the roots of a tree, they found a small, sturdy door with a bell-pull and a brass plate bearing a name.

Rat hauled upon the bell-pull with all his might, and after a long, anxious wait they heard slow, shuffling footsteps and a gruff voice demanding who dared to disturb honest folk on such a night. When the door was opened by a stout, grey old animal in a dressing gown, and his sharp little eyes took in the shivering pair upon his step, his frown melted at once. “Come in, both of you,” he said, and bundled them into the warm passage before another word could be spoken.

In his great stone-floored kitchen, where a log fire blazed and hams hung from the rafters, Badger set the travellers down, dried them and gave them slippers and a plain, hearty supper. Over the meal he explained that the Wild Wood had once been a thriving city, and that its people had long ago vanished, leaving their broken streets for the earth to swallow. His own tunnels and passages wound beneath it all, he said, so that nothing above could ever trouble him.

In the morning, after a hearty breakfast, Badger led his guests along a long, low passage that wound beneath the wood and brought them out at last on the sunny edge of the fields. Here, for the first time, he spoke of Toad, and he said that the animal's recklessness could no longer be ignored. When spring came, he promised, they would all take Toad in hand together, and the madness for motor cars would be cured.

Some weeks later, as they walked home through the frosty dusk past a village, Mole stopped dead in the lane. A faint but unmistakable smell drifted towards him, the smell of his own old home, abandoned in the first rush of spring, and it called to him as plainly as a voice. Rat, who had been walking ahead, was too absorbed to notice, and before Mole could say a word he was shaken by a great sob.

Rat came hurrying back, listened with warm sympathy, and without a moment's hesitation turned to follow the scent. They hunted among the hedges until, in the snow, they discovered the little doorway of Mole's own home. Inside it was dusty, cold and shabby, with cobwebs in the corners, yet Mole, drawing the cloths from his dear old furniture, found that it looked precisely as he remembered it.

As they lit the lamps, a thin sound of voices rose outside, and a little troop of field mice appeared in the snow, singing a Christmas carol by the light of their lanterns. Mole, who had almost nothing in the cupboard, sent Rat out to buy supper, and between them they fed the singers on warm drinks and the best food that could be found. The small guests went away in high spirits, and the two friends sat down to their own meal with the happy feeling of a good deed done.

When supper was over and the fire had died low, Mole sat looking round at his humble room, and at last he understood what it meant to have a home of his own. He had enjoyed the river and the open road, and he was grateful for Rat and for all that had befallen him, yet he knew now that nothing could replace this small, familiar place. Then he crept into his old bed and slept peacefully, with the whole world safe and quiet beyond the door.

Spring passed and summer came, but Toad's mania for motor cars grew more extravagant by the month. He had crashed car after car, been fined and hauled before the magistrates, and spent a fortune on hospitals and repairs without seeming to learn anything from the experience. At last Badger arrived at Rat's door, grave as a judge, and announced that the time for gentle words had passed and that Toad must be saved from himself.

The three friends marched up to Toad Hall, where they found their friend admiring himself in a flamboyant new driving coat, goggles and gaiters, quite ready to set out for another drive. Badger told him sternly that his behaviour was a disgrace and that he must give it up, but Toad merely smiled and refused to promise anything. They therefore carried him bodily upstairs, locked him in his own bedroom and resolved to take turns guarding him until he came to his senses.

Toad, however, was never short of cunning, and one afternoon, while Rat sat watching him, he declared himself dangerously ill and begged for a doctor. The kind-hearted Rat, anxious and half persuaded, hurried off to fetch one, whereupon Toad knotted the sheets and blankets together, tied them to the window frame and slid down to freedom. Soon he was strolling happily along the road, shaking with laughter at his own cleverness and more pleased with himself than ever.

Wandering into a village, he went into the inn for a hearty lunch, and there, in the yard outside, a magnificent motor car stood waiting with no one in charge of it. The temptation proved too much for him, and, creeping out, he cranked the engine, climbed into the seat and tore away along the country roads in a glorious frenzy of speed. He had gone only a short distance before the police, who had been alerted, overtook him and dragged him from the driver's seat.

He was tried at the town hall and convicted of three crimes: stealing a motor car, driving at a furious and dangerous speed, and being grossly impertinent to the police. The magistrate, who showed no mercy, added up the sentences and condemned him to twenty years in prison. Toad was led down to the deepest dungeon of an ancient castle, and as the heavy bolts slid home behind him he felt that the sun would never shine on him again.

In the dark, cold cell, Toad flung himself on the stone floor and wept bitterly, certain that he would be forgotten and that Toad Hall would crumble without its master. Yet the jailer's daughter, a gentle girl who loved animals, could not bear to hear him, and she began to bring him cups of tea and hot buttered toast. Little by little she coaxed him back to hope, and he told her all about his house, his riches and his marvellous talents.

One day she told him that her aunt, a washerwoman, called at the prison every week to collect the linen, and she offered a daring plan. Toad was to put on the old woman's gown, shawl and bonnet, take her washing and walk out past the guards, who would never suspect him. It worked like a charm: the soldiers laughed and joked as Toad passed, and in a moment he was through the gate and free.

At the station Toad found that he had too little money for a ticket, but the driver of the train, touched by his sad story, let him ride on the engine. Before long a wild pursuit began, for the police had discovered his escape and set off in another engine, with officers clinging to its sides. Toad and the driver shovelled coal until their faces were black, and when the train dived into a tunnel he leapt off and hid in the woods while the pursuers thundered by.

Midsummer had come to the river, and Otter, who was usually the cheeriest of friends, sat waiting anxiously at the shallows, for his young son Portly had vanished. Rat and Mole, hearing of it, set out at dusk in the boat, promising to search every creek and backwater until the little fellow was found. A tender moonlight lay over the water, and the hedges and willows stood motionless as though the whole world were holding its breath.

All night they rowed from bank to bank, calling softly and searching every island and stream, while the stars wheeled slowly overhead. Then, as the sky grew pale before the dawn, Rat stopped rowing and listened, for a melody of unearthly sweetness was drifting down the river. Mole heard it too, and both felt themselves drawn irresistibly towards a small island in the stream, as though some great, kind hand were guiding the boat.

There, among the willows and the wild roses, they came upon a vision which neither could ever afterwards describe, the great horned figure of Pan, friend and helper of the small beasts, with little Portly sleeping peacefully against his hooves. Rat and Mole bowed their heads in awe, and yet their fear was not of harm but of something too tremendous for words. When the vision faded they had been granted the gift of forgetting, and they remembered only a vague and lovely music as they rowed Portly home to his father.

Toad, meanwhile, still dressed as a washerwoman, begged a ride on a barge drawn by a heavy horse, and the stout woman who owned it agreed if he would wash a few of her things. But Toad had never washed so much as a handkerchief in his life, and his soapy, clumsy attempts soon convinced the woman that her passenger was no washerwoman at all. The argument ended with Toad scrambling onto the horse's back and galloping away along the towpath, leaving the woman shouting after him.

He rode on across the countryside until, tired and hungry, he sold the horse to a passing traveller for a few shillings and a hot breakfast from the man's own stew pot. Having eaten as much as he could hold, he trudged along the road with money in his pocket, boasting to himself about his own astonishing cleverness and fancying that the whole world admired him. Pride, as the old saying goes, comes before a fall, and Toad, light-hearted as ever, was about to find out how true that is.

Presently a motor car came purring along the road, and the kindly owners, taking him for a tired old washerwoman, drew up and offered her a seat. The sight of the gleaming bonnet and the hum of the engine were too much for Toad, who forgot every lesson of his sorrows, seized the wheel and sent the car racing across the countryside. A moment later it left the road, flew across a meadow and plunged into a deep pond, while Toad, flung high into the air, splashed into the water and scrambled out half-drowned.

Autumn had come to the river bank, the leaves were turning gold and brown, and flocks of swallows gathered on the roofs in noisy conferences, restless to be away. Rat, who had always been content to stay at home, watched them with a curious ache, for something in him seemed to answer their call to the sunny south. Mole noticed that his friend was distracted and silent, but he did not yet understand what was happening in his heart.

One evening a travel-stained stranger knocked at the door, a lean Sea Rat from the harbours of the south, who sat before the fire and began to talk. He spoke of galleys and white-sailed ships, of ports where fruit and spices lay piled on the quays, of storms at sea and of lands where the sun never ceased to shine. Rat, spellbound, listened with burning cheeks, and each fresh story fell like a spark into the dry timber of his longing.

In the morning the spell was complete: Rat packed a few belongings, buckled on a pack and made ready to follow the Sea Rat, with the cool calmness of one walking in his sleep. Mole, however, was not deceived, and standing firmly in the doorway he held his friend back with gentle strength until the fever had passed. Then, understanding what Rat needed, he put a pencil into his hand and set him to writing verses, and by evening the sea and the south had been exchanged for rhymes and a quiet content.

When the weather turned wet and cold, a dreadful figure dragged itself through the doorway of Rat's home, a tattered, muddy and shivering Toad, home at last after his long run of misfortune. Rat gave him a bath, a change of clothes and a hot meal, and listened with half a smile to the story of his escape. But when he told Toad that a horde of weasels, stoats and ferrets from the Wild Wood had seized Toad Hall and installed themselves in its splendid rooms, Toad's face fell and the boasting stopped altogether.

Toad dissolved into sobs, for tears came as readily to him as laughter, and he wept for his house, his treasures and his foolish pride. Rat comforted him as best he could, and when Badger came in soon afterwards, he spoke to Toad with stern kindness and told him that no good would come of bravado. There was a way, the old Badger added, to win the Hall back, but it would take cunning, courage and perfect silence, and Toad must for once do as he was told.

First, however, they needed information, and Mole, who was always eager to be of use, borrowed a disguise and slipped away through the dusk to spy upon the Hall. He crept close to the gates and the windows, listened to the careless talk of the sentries and heard that the Chief Weasel was giving a great banquet for his followers that very night. He hurried back at full speed to tell his friends that the guard was lax, that the weasels were confident, and that no better opportunity would ever be offered.

Badger now leaned forward and explained that a secret passage led from the river bank right up to the pantry of Toad Hall. Toad was thunderstruck, for in all the years he had lived in his own house he had never so much as guessed that it was there. Nobody who knew the weasels' habits, said Badger, would expect an enemy to arrive from under the floor.

Late that night, armed with cudgels and a sense of purpose, the four friends made their way down to the river bank where the passage began, and Badger led them down into the earth. The tunnel was long, narrow and pitch-black, and its damp floor and low roof forced even the sturdy Badger to stoop. Toad, bursting with plans and boasts, was hushed more than once by his stern companion, who knew that a single careless word would ruin everything.

At the far end a flight of steps led up to a trapdoor, and above their heads rose a muffled roar of singing, banging and bursts of coarse laughter. The weasels and stoats had been feasting for hours, and the Chief Weasel was making a long and rambling speech that no one seemed able to stop. Not one of the revellers suspected that, only a few feet below, four fierce avengers were waiting in the darkness for Badger's signal.

At the word from Badger they flung open the trap and burst into the hall with a roar that shook the rafters, each of them brandishing a stick and shouting at the top of his voice. The terrified weasels, thinking that a whole army had fallen upon them out of the earth, dropped their glasses, overturned the tables and fled in all directions. Within minutes the great hall rang with squeals, crashes and the thud of sticks, and every plate and chair had been flung across the room.

Those who could not escape through the doors leapt out of the windows, and the rest surrendered in a heap, begging for mercy, while Badger stood in the middle of the room like a general who has won his battle. In the stillness that followed, the four friends looked round at the broken glass and overturned tables, and then, laughing and exhausted, they shook hands. Toad Hall, battered but undefeated, was at last restored to its rightful master, and the long nightmare of exile had ended.

The next day the friends held a magnificent banquet in the restored hall, with lanterns glowing in every window and the table groaning under dishes of every kind. Toad, who had learned something at last from his troubles, kept his boasting in check, spoke modestly of his friends' courage and thanked them one by one. From that evening he was a changed animal, and the river bank was quiet and happy again, with the four friends enjoying the long evenings together.
